Sherlock Jr. Buster Keaton's 1924 comedy about a movie projectionist who dreams himself into the screen of a film noir he is showing, becoming a detective confronting criminals, supernatural perils, and impossible physics. Layering dreams within cinema, it is a formal masterpiece that plays with the medium's ontology while delivering brilliant visual comedy and dangerous physical stunts.

Directed by Buster Keaton and Roscoe Arbuckle, the transition into the film happens when Keaton's character falls asleep in the projection booth and his dream-self enters the cinema screen. The layering of reality and fiction becomes Keaton's conceptual playground. The dream-film itself is a parody detective noir where Sherlock Jr. must pursue jewel thieves while the environment transforms around him. A door opens onto a garden, which becomes a seaside cliff, which becomes a snowfield.

Keaton's famous stunt involved the front of a house facade collapsing around him. Only a window opening remained to save him from being crushed. He performed this with no safety net or special effects. The poolside chase involves Keaton's signature physical precision: running across a log while it spins in the water, landing perfectly in a rowboat, all without breaking his stone-faced composure.

Visual gags rely on the film-within-a-film conceit. Keaton's character discovers his actions on-screen don't correspond to his intentions, playing with audience expectations. The ending blurs reality and dream. Is Keaton still dreaming? Has cinema and waking life become indistinguishable? It remains one of the most formally inventive comedies of the silent era, demonstrating comedy's power independent of dialogue.
